Can a squatter take ownership of a house?

Only by occupying it openly and continuously for a long statutory period, and a few weeks or months in a vacant house comes nowhere near that. North Carolina sets 20 years of adverse possession under known and visible lines and boundaries, or seven years if the occupant also holds color of title (G.S. 1-40 and G.S. 1-38).

Both statutes speak of persons not under disability, so the bar does not run the same way against someone who is. The time limits protect the occupant only if the possession meets the statute's conditions the whole way through.

The 7-year and 20-year rules

The main difference is the paper the occupant holds. Seven years of possession works only with color of title, which means a document that appears to convey the land. Twenty years does not require one.

Adverse possession periods in North Carolina
RulePeriodWhat the occupant must show
Color of title (G.S. 1-38)7 yearsPossession under known and visible lines and boundaries and under color of title
Without color of title (G.S. 1-40)20 yearsPossession under known and visible lines and boundaries, adverse to all other persons

Under the seven-year rule, a person with a right to the land who does not sue within seven years after that right accrued is shut out from any later claim. A completed possession is a perpetual bar against persons not under disability. The statute also provides that commissioner's deeds from judicial sales and trustee's deeds from foreclosure count as color of title.

Known and visible lines and boundaries

The phrase means the occupant has to claim a definite piece of land that others can see. Subsection (b) of G.S. 1-38 gives one way to prove it: mark the boundaries, record a survey map, and list and pay the taxes on the property.

  • Boundaries are marked with distinctive marks on trees or by visible metal or concrete markers, visible to a height of 18 inches above the ground.
  • A map prepared from an actual survey by a North Carolina registered surveyor is recorded in the book of maps in the register of deeds office in the county.
  • The map carries the surveyor's certificate that the boundaries match the deed or other title instrument, with its book and page or file number.
  • Listing and paying taxes on that marked and surveyed land is then prima facie evidence of possession under known and visible lines and boundaries.

An owner who keeps paying the property tax and has a current recorded survey is in a stronger position than one who has neither. Check your records at the register of deeds and the county tax office.

Squatter or trespasser?

The criminal law treats both the same way: entering or staying on someone's land or building without authorization is trespass. First degree trespass covers entering or remaining in the building of another, or on premises enclosed or secured to show an intent to keep intruders out. It is a Class 2 misdemeanor (G.S. 14-159.12).

Two situations raise it to a Class I felony with a fine of at least $1,000. One is returning to land after being removed under a valid order or writ for possession. The other is acting under color of title after knowingly creating or giving materially false evidence of an ownership or possessory interest. This second one is aimed at fake deeds and leases used to claim a house that is not theirs.

Second degree trespass applies when a person remains after the owner, an occupant or another authorized person says to leave, or on posted premises, and it is a Class 3 misdemeanor (G.S. 14-159.13). Entering the curtilage of a dwelling between midnight and 6:00 a.m. is a Class 2 misdemeanor.

Removing someone who claims to rent

If the person is a tenant or claims to be one, the route is summary ejectment in small claims court, not self-help. Grounds under G.S. 42-26 include holding over after the term ends, breaching a lease condition that ends the estate, and leaving while rent is owed. Past-due water, sewer or electric charges cannot be the basis for ending a lease.

Notice periods depend on the kind of tenancy under G.S. 42-14.

  • Year to year: notice at least one month before the end of the current year.
  • Month to month: seven days.
  • Week to week: two days.
  • Manufactured home space rental: at least 60 days before the end of the current rental period.

For unpaid rent, the lease term is forfeited when rent is not paid within 10 days after demand for all past-due rent (G.S. 42-3). Small claims charges a $96 filing fee and a $30 sheriff service fee, and eviction hearings are usually set within 10 to 15 days. Either side may appeal to district court within 10 days of the magistrate's decision.

How to prevent an adverse possession claim

Prevention is mostly about attention and paper. A claimant has to occupy the land continuously, openly and against everyone else, which is hard to do on land the owner visits and uses. A vacant house or an unvisited lot is where an occupant's use can go unchallenged longest.

  • Inspect vacant property on a regular schedule and keep dated photos.
  • Tell trespassers in writing to leave, and keep a copy. A written notice supports a second degree trespass complaint.
  • Post no-trespassing notices where they are likely to be seen.
  • Keep paying and listing the property tax so your name stays on the county record.
  • Record a survey if a neighbor's fence, shed or driveway crosses your line.
  • Ask an attorney about a lawsuit for possession if someone has been on the land for years.
Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy North Carolina houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Selling a house someone is occupying

An owner can still sell, but the occupant has to be dealt with in the contract. Whoever buys the house will ask who lives there and on what terms.

Tell the closing attorney who is living there, how long, and what documents they hold. The contract should say who is responsible for removal and by when. Do not remove belongings or change locks on someone who claims tenancy without first getting advice from a North Carolina attorney, since that can bring its own liability. A cash buyer may accept a house with an occupant, but expect the price and closing date to reflect the risk.

Frequently asked questions

How long does adverse possession take in North Carolina?

Twenty years under G.S. 1-40, or seven years if the occupant also has color of title under G.S. 1-38. In both cases the possession must be under known and visible lines and boundaries.

What is color of title?

It is a document that appears to give the occupant title but does not actually do so. G.S. 1-38 also treats commissioner's deeds in judicial sales and trustee's deeds under foreclosure as color of title.

Is squatting a crime in North Carolina?

Often yes. Remaining in another person's building without authorization is first degree trespass, a Class 2 misdemeanor, and remaining after being told to leave is second degree trespass, a Class 3 misdemeanor.

Can I change the locks to remove a tenant?

No, not if the person is a tenant or claims to be. The path is a summary ejectment case in small claims, after proper notice for the type of tenancy. Ask an attorney before you act.

Does paying property tax matter for adverse possession?

It can. G.S. 1-38(b) makes listing and paying taxes on marked and surveyed property prima facie evidence of possession under known and visible lines and boundaries, so an owner who pays keeps the stronger record.

title: North Carolina Landlord Tenant Law and Tenant Rights: Rules for Selling a Rental
content:
North Carolina Landlord Tenant Law and Tenant Rights: Rules for Selling a Rental

Cash Home Buyers in North Carolina
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • North Carolina Landlord Tenant Law and Tenant Rights: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a North Carolina Landlord Tenant Law and Tenant Rights sale
  • Turn the North Carolina Landlord Tenant Law and Tenant Rights offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling a North Carolina House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in North Carolina?
We buy North Carolina houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

If the landlord sells the rental

A tenant's deposit follows the property. When a landlord's interest ends through a sale, an assignment, a death or a receiver's appointment, G.S. 42-54 gives the landlord 30 days to deal with it.

The seller can do one of two things. The first is to hand the unspent deposit to the buyer and mail the tenant a notice that names the buyer and gives an address. The second is to refund the tenant directly. Either route ends the seller's liability for that money. A buyer who takes over tenants should leave closing with the deposit ledger, the leases and any written repair requests.

Security deposit limits

The cap depends on the length of the tenancy. Section 42-51(b) allows two weeks' rent on a weekly tenancy, a month and a half of rent on a monthly one, and two months' rent on any longer term.

  • Deposits can cover unpaid rent and certain water, sewer or electric charges.
  • They can cover damage to the unit, including damaged smoke or carbon monoxide alarms.
  • They can cover re-renting costs after a breach, including a broker's reasonable fee.
  • They can cover removing and storing belongings after a summary ejectment case, plus court costs.

Within a month after the tenancy ends and the keys come back, the landlord owes the tenant a written, itemized accounting. If a claim is still unsettled at that point, the landlord sends an interim report then and a final one by day 60. Ordinary wear and tear cannot be charged, and the amount kept cannot exceed actual damages.

Repairs a landlord must make

The landlord has to keep the home fit and habitable, and G.S. 42-42(a) lists the duties. They include following building and housing codes, keeping common areas safe, and maintaining electrical, plumbing, heating and cooling systems. Repairs should follow promptly once the tenant gives written notice, except in emergencies.

The statute also requires working smoke alarms, repaired or replaced within fifteen days after the tenant writes to the landlord. Units with a fuel-burning heater, appliance or fireplace, or an attached garage, need at least one carbon monoxide alarm per level. A landlord who installs or replaces a smoke alarm must use a tamper-resistant model with a 10-year lithium battery, unless the unit has a hardwired alarm with battery backup or a combined smoke and carbon monoxide alarm. Imminently dangerous conditions must be fixed within a reasonable time. Examples are unsafe wiring or steps, no potable water, no operable toilet and, from November 1 through March 31, no heating that can reach 65 degrees when it is 20 degrees outside.

A tenant cannot waive these duties by accepting a bad unit. If you are selling, treat open code or alarm problems as part of what the buyer inherits, and ask the county inspections office what is on file.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your North Carolina house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Can a landlord retaliate for repair requests?

No. G.S. 42-37.1 protects good-faith repair requests, complaints to a government agency, formal complaints by a government authority, efforts to enforce lease or legal rights, and joining a tenants' organization.

In a summary ejectment case, a tenant can raise retaliation as a defense by showing that the landlord's action substantially responds to one of those acts within 12 months before filing. The landlord can still win in several situations: the tenant breached the rent covenant or another substantial lease term, a fixed term ended without a renewal option, the tenant mainly caused the violation, code compliance requires emptying the unit, a good-faith notice to quit was delivered earlier, or the owner sincerely wants the home to live in, plans a remodel that displaces the household, or will take it off the rental market for six months or longer.

Notice periods by tenancy type

Notice to end a North Carolina tenancy (G.S. 42-14, 42-3 and 42-26)
Tenancy typeNotice or step required
Yearly leaseA month or more before the year runs out
Monthly leaseSeven days
Weekly leaseTwo days
Manufactured home lot60 days or more ahead of the period's end
Unpaid rentTerm forfeited when past-due rent stays unpaid 10 days after a demand

Summary ejectment under G.S. 42-26 covers holding over after the term, breaking a condition that ends the estate, and leaving while rent is owed. Back charges for water, sewer or electric service are not grounds for ending a lease.

How an eviction case moves through court

The landlord files in small claims before a magistrate. Hearings are set within a month of filing, and eviction cases often get a date in 10 to 15 days. The court system lists a $96 filing fee and a $30 sheriff service fee, and small claims has no jury.

  • A defendant served fewer than two days before the hearing is entitled to a continuance.
  • Either side can appeal to district court, orally in the courtroom or in writing, within ten days after the magistrate rules.
  • Appeal costs must be paid, and a bond may be required to stop enforcement.

An owner who wants the house empty should plan around that timeline. Changing locks or removing belongings without a court order is no shortcut. Eviction here goes through the court and the sheriff.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy North Carolina houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Tenants when a lender forecloses

Tenants in a foreclosed rental get some breathing room. A notice of sale for a residential building with fewer than fifteen rental units must say that an order for possession may issue. A tenant whose lease was signed or renewed on or after October 1, 2007 may end it on 10 to 90 days' notice, counted from the sale date.

After a sale is reported, anyone can submit an upset bid within 10 days if it tops the last bid by at least 5% and at least $750. Each upset bid restarts the 10-day period and pushes the final date back, so tenants should watch the court file for the confirmed sale.

Before you list a rental

Begin with the lease file. Write down each tenant's term, the deposit held and the date a notice to quit could take effect. Then decide between selling with tenants in place or delivering an empty house.

If tenants stay, give the buyer the deposit records so the 30-day transfer duty is met. If the unit will be empty, work through the notice periods and the court process, and give a monthly tenant at least the seven days the statute requires. Have a local attorney review the plan if a repair complaint is open, since a retaliation defense can slow a case.

Sellers who do not want to manage a notice period, a court date and a deposit accounting sometimes choose a cash buyer who takes the property with the tenants or the vacancy as it stands. Compare that route against the time and cost of the steps above.

Frequently asked questions

When must a landlord return a security deposit?

By mail or hand delivery, with an itemized damage list and the balance, no later than 30 days after the tenancy ends and possession returns. An unsettled claim needs an interim accounting by then and a final one by day 60.

How high can a deposit go?

Two weeks' rent on a weekly tenancy, one and a half months' on a monthly one, and two months' on longer terms.

How much warning does a monthly tenant get?

Seven days. Weekly tenancies need two days, and yearly ones a month or more before the year ends.

Who holds the deposit after the landlord sells?

Within 30 days the seller must either pass it to the new owner and notify the tenant by mail, or refund it to the tenant.

Can a tenant stay after a foreclosure sale?

For a while. Sale notices for small residential rentals must warn that a possession order may issue, and tenants under qualifying leases may end the lease on 10 to 90 days' notice after the sale date.

title: North Carolina Eviction Notice Rules: Notice Types, Days and Selling the House
content:
North Carolina Eviction Notice Rules: Notice Types, Days and Selling the House

Cash Home Buyers in North Carolina
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • North Carolina Eviction Notice Rules: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a North Carolina Eviction Notice Rules sale
  • Turn the North Carolina Eviction Notice Rules offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling a North Carolina House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in North Carolina?
We buy North Carolina houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

Written notices a landlord can use

Three tools exist. A notice to quit ends a periodic tenancy. A demand for past-due rent starts a ten-day clock. A lease breach or holdover supports a court complaint without any set number of days beyond what the lease says.

The rules sit in Chapter 42 of the General Statutes: 42-14 covers ending a tenancy, 42-3 covers rent demands, and 42-26 lists the grounds a court will hear.

An owner who plans to sell a rented house should pick the right tool first, because the choice sets the earliest date the house can be handed over empty.

Notice periods by tenancy type

The length of the notice tracks the length of the rental period. Weekly tenants get the least time and annual tenants the most.

Notice to quit under G.S. 42-14
Type of tenancyNotice required
Year to yearAt least one month before the current year ends
Month to monthSeven days
Week to weekTwo days
Space rental for a manufactured homeAt least 60 days before the current rental period ends

A written lease with a fixed end date follows other logic: a tenant who stays past the term is a holdover, which is one of the grounds in G.S. 42-26. Read the lease for added notice terms before counting days.

When rent goes unpaid

The landlord demands every dollar of past-due rent. If the tenant lets ten days pass without paying, the lease term is forfeited and the landlord may re-enter through the courts. G.S. 42-3 speaks to leases that fix a date for rent.

Late fees run on a separate track under G.S. 42-46. Rent must be five calendar days late before any fee applies, counting the day after the due date as day one. Monthly rent allows fifteen dollars or five percent of the rent, whichever is greater, and weekly rent allows four dollars or five percent on the same terms. One fee per late payment is the limit.

  • A late fee cannot be subtracted from next month's rent in a way that puts that rent in default.
  • No late fee may be charged for water or sewer service provided under G.S. 62-110(g).
  • On subsidized rent, fees are figured on the tenant's share alone.
Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your North Carolina house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Other grounds for a complaint

G.S. 42-26 names three: staying past the end of the term, breaking a lease condition that terminates the estate, and deserting the home while owing rent. Any other complaint needs a fresh read of the lease and the statute.

One limit surprises landlords who provide utilities. Unpaid water, sewer or electric charges may not be the basis for ending a lease, so collect that money another way.

A breach claim is strongest when the lease states the condition and the consequence in plain words. Keep the lease, any written demand, the delivery dates and proof of delivery. The magistrate decides by a preponderance of the evidence under G.S. 42-30, so paper matters.

After the notice period runs

The landlord files a complaint, and under G.S. 42-28 the clerk issues a summons naming a court date no more than seven days out, weekends and legal holidays excluded.

Small claims dates fall within 30 days of filing, and eviction cases are usually heard within 10 to 15 days. Our eviction process page follows the case from the complaint to the sheriff.

When the magistrate awards possession, the sheriff carries out the writ. The sheriff must warn the tenant of the approximate time, and the writ must be executed within five days of reaching the sheriff, under G.S. 42-36.2.

What a tenant can pay to cure a default

A tenant who cures can end the case early, and the cure amount may include more than rent. Under G.S. 42-46, the landlord may fold court filing fees, the cost of serving process and out-of-pocket litigation expenses into the figure needed to cure a default.

Reasonable attorney fees can be added too, if a written lease provides for them, up to fifteen percent of the amount owed, or fifteen percent of the monthly rent when the default is something other than unpaid rent. A written lease may also allow a complaint-filing fee of fifteen dollars or five percent of monthly rent, whichever is greater, when the tenant cures and the landlord dismisses before judgment.

Only one administrative fee may be kept for a single complaint, and the landlord cannot deduct that fee from later rent or call its nonpayment a new default. If you plan to sell, a cure that ends in a dismissed case can leave the tenant in place, so tell the buyer in writing.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy North Carolina houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Timeline before a sale can close

Add the pieces together. The notice period comes first, the court date follows within days, and the sheriff's window comes last.

  • Notice period from the table above, or ten days after a rent demand.
  • A summons date no more than seven days after issuance.
  • A hearing that is usually held within 10 to 15 days of filing.
  • Ten days for a tenant to appeal the magistrate's decision, which can delay enforcement if a bond is posted.
  • Up to five days for the sheriff to execute the writ.

These steps overlap in places, but a buyer who needs the house vacant should be told that each one can add time.

How notices affect a landlord who wants to sell

Each tenancy type runs on its own clock, so the closing date has to be built around it. A buyer who wants a vacant house needs the notice period, the hearing and any appeal to fit before closing.

  • For a monthly tenancy, seven days ends the tenancy on paper, and removal of anyone who stays goes through the court.
  • For a yearly tenancy, the notice has to arrive a month or more before the year ends.
  • For a manufactured home space, plan on 60 days or more before the rental period ends.

A foreclosure sale shifts the clock. Under G.S. 45-21.16A, a tenant whose rental agreement began or renewed on October 1, 2007 or later may end it on 10 to 90 days' notice after the sale date. The notice of sale for a residential property with fewer than 15 rental units must also warn that an order for possession may issue.

What to record before serving a notice

Write down the tenancy type, the rental period, the due date and the date of each payment, then match them to the table and to the ground you plan to use.

  • Which tenancy applies and its notice period.
  • Any lease terms that go beyond the statute.
  • The date and method of delivery for the notice or rent demand.
  • Whether any of the amount owed is water, sewer or electric arrears.
  • Whether a fee you plan to charge fits G.S. 42-46.

The clerk of superior court in your county can supply the current complaint form and filing steps. A landlord-tenant attorney can review the notice before it is served.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

What notice ends a monthly rental in North Carolina?

Seven days. G.S. 42-14 also sets two days for a weekly tenancy and at least one month before year end for a yearly one.

How soon must a tenant pay once the landlord demands the rent?

Within ten days. G.S. 42-3 forfeits the lease term if the past-due rent stays unpaid after that, and the landlord may then re-enter.

Can unpaid electric or water charges end a lease?

No. G.S. 42-26 bars arrears for water, sewer or electric service from serving as the basis for termination.

What notice does a manufactured home lot renter get?

At least 60 days before the end of the rental period, under G.S. 42-14.

May a landlord lock the tenant out after serving notice?

No. Possession comes through a court judgment and a sheriff's writ. The clerk sets the court date within seven days of the summons under G.S. 42-28.

What happens when property tax goes unpaid

The taxing unit holds a lien on the parcel, advertises it, and may then force a court-supervised sale. Chapter 105 of the General Statutes lays out each stage. The owner can end the process by paying what is owed, up to a cutoff that depends on which foreclosure route the unit picked.

Counties and towns run these sales themselves. Their tax collector places the ad, a court case or a docketed judgment follows, and either a commissioner or the sheriff auctions the parcel. An owner who wants any say in the price has to act before that sale is scheduled.

The lien dates from the day the property was to be listed for tax, and G.S. 105-355 attaches penalties, interest and costs to it from that moment. Bills fall due September 1. Payment before January 6 carries no interest. After that, G.S. 105-360 adds 2 percent until February 1 and then 0.75 percent for every month, or part of a month, still unpaid.

How the lien is advertised

Liens are advertised from March 1 through June 30. Under G.S. 105-369 the collector reports unpaid real property tax to the governing body in February: the county report is due the first Monday, the city or town report the second Monday.

A month or more before the ad runs, the collector mails the record owner a first-class letter. The notice states the unpaid principal and warns that the owner's name will appear in a newspaper ad. A mistake in mailing that notice does not void the lien or a later foreclosure, so an owner who moved should keep the tax office updated.

  • A county posts its list at the courthouse and prints each lien at least once in a local paper; a city posts at city or town hall.
  • The ad lists the record owner as of the delinquency date, a short parcel description and the principal amount, and warns that interest and costs will be added.
  • Each advertised parcel carries an advertising fee that counts as tax.
  • A parcel comes off the list when the owner pays the tax, accrued interest and a share of the advertising fee during the advertising period.

The two foreclosure routes

A taxing unit can sue to foreclose under G.S. 105-374, or it can docket a certificate of taxes as a judgment under G.S. 105-375. The governing body decides which route applies, so ask the collector about your parcel.

The 105-374 route is a court action filed in the county where the land lies, in the nature of a mortgage foreclosure. The owner of record, the spouse and other lienholders are served. The 105-375 route is the in rem alternative, described in the statute as a simple and inexpensive way to enforce taxes. The comparison below sets the two side by side.

How G.S. 105-374 and G.S. 105-375 differ on the points that affect an owner
PointG.S. 105-374 actionG.S. 105-375 judgment

Notice to ownerService on owner, spouse and lienholdersCertified or registered mail at least 30 days before docketing, with follow-up posting or newspaper notice if no receipt returns in 10 days
Added costsCommissioner fee up to 5 percent of the purchase priceMailing and publication costs plus a $250 administrative charge
SalePublic auction at the courthouse doorSheriff sale on execution, issued after three months and before two years from indexing

What happens at the sale

The property goes to the highest bidder at public auction, and the buyer receives fee simple title free of most liens. In a 105-374 sale the commissioner may ask bidders for a deposit of as much as a fifth of the bid, and the commissioner reports the result within three days. A ten day window then opens for exceptions or a higher bid, and confirmation can be sought after it closes.

Under 105-375 the sheriff sells as in any execution sale, with two differences. The owner gets no debtor's exemption, and the sheriff must send certified or registered mail to the taxpayer and each recorded lienholder a month before the auction. The buyer takes the property free of claims except other unpaid taxes or special assessments, C-PACE assessments and conservation agreements.

The 105-375 route also takes a clerk's fee out of the sale proceeds. Attorney fees for the taxing unit are arranged separately and cannot be added to the judgment as costs.

Redeeming the property or stopping the sale

An owner can do both. In a 105-374 action, whoever redeems before confirmation pays the taxes, penalties, interest and costs, and whatever the sale brought in beyond the tax goes to the court for those entitled to it. In a 105-375 case, the owner or anyone with an interest can ask the clerk to set the judgment aside before execution issues if the tax was paid or the lien is invalid, and paying the judgment in full ends it.

  • Pay before the advertisement: the parcel never appears on the list.
  • Pay after the ad runs: add the accrued interest and a share of the advertising fee.
  • Pay after a judgment is docketed: add interest at 8 percent plus the costs and the $250 charge.
  • Pay before confirmation in a 105-374 sale: add penalties, interest and all costs.

Because the amounts change at each stage, ask the tax collector for a written payoff figure with an end date. A title company will want that number too if you sell.

If the county or city buys the property

A taxing unit may bid at the sale, and if it wins it can resell the parcel later. G.S. 105-376 lets the unit pay only the part of its bid that would not go back to the taxing units as tax, penalties, interest and costs. It then holds the property for every unit with an interest and uses net income and resale money first to repay its own outlay.

The same statute allows a resale by private sale to the former owner or another person who had an interest, for an amount not less than the unit's interest, if the governing body approves. Ask the tax office whether it entertains that kind of offer before assuming the auction ended your options.

Selling before a tax foreclosure sale

A private sale lets you choose the timing and keep any value above the debt. At auction the price is whatever the room bids, and the costs above come off the top.

  • Collect a payoff statement from every taxing unit, since a county and a town can each hold a lien on one parcel.
  • File the deed promptly: G.S. 47-18 protects a buyer against creditors only from the moment of registration.
  • Plan for the seller's deed tax under G.S. 105-228.30, a dollar per $500 of price, handed to the register with the deed.
  • Recording fees come from G.S. 161-10, with a 15 page deed starting at $26.

If the house needs work, has tenants, or came through an estate, a buyer who takes it as is can simplify the payoff. Ask the closing agent to settle the tax out of the proceeds, and the register of deeds will file the new deed.

Frequently asked questions

Does North Carolina sell tax liens to investors?

The statutes provide for foreclosure and sale of the property itself, with the taxing unit as lienholder and the buyer taking title at the sale. They set out no certificate sale to private investors, so ask your county tax collector how it collects delinquent real estate tax.

When are unpaid property taxes advertised?

The ads run from March 1 through June 30. In February the collector reports unpaid real property tax to the governing body, the owner gets a mailed warning ahead of publication, and the list is posted and printed.

Can I still pay after the lien is advertised?

Yes. During the advertising period a parcel comes off the list when the owner pays the tax, accrued interest and a share of the advertising fee. After a foreclosure starts, paying taxes, penalties, interest and costs still ends it before confirmation under 105-374, or before execution under 105-375.

Does the buyer at a tax sale get a clean title?

Mostly, yes. The buyer takes fee simple title free of most claims and liens. Other unpaid taxes or special assessments, C-PACE assessments and conservation agreements can survive, so a buyer should ask a title company about them.

What does the 105-375 judgment cost an owner on top of the tax?

The judgment adds interest at 8 percent a year, the mailing and publication costs and a $250 administrative charge. A tax collector can give the exact total for your parcel on a given date.
